name: Wheat Stem Rust
affected_hosts: Primarily affects wheat, but also infects barley and some wild grasses.
symptoms: Brick-red pustules on stems and leaf sheaths
Pustules rupture the epidermis, releasing powdery spores
Severe infection leads to shriveled grains and lodging
conditions: Warm, humid conditions with extended dew periods favor disease development and spore dissemination.
cycle: The fungus overwinters as teliospores, which germinate in spring to produce basidiospores that infect alternate hosts (barberry), then aeciospores infect wheat, completing the cycle with urediniospores spreading rapidly.
diagnosis: Visual inspection for characteristic brick-red pustules and microscopic examination of spores confirm the presence of the pathogen.
impact: Can cause devastating yield losses, historically leading to famines if susceptible varieties are widely planted.
prevention: Planting resistant varieties is the most effective and economical prevention strategy.
chemical: Application based on disease forecasting models
ipm: Integrates resistant varieties, timely fungicide applications, and monitoring of disease spread to minimize economic impact.
geography: Globally distributed, particularly problematic in major wheat-growing regions of Africa, Asia, and North America.
differential: Distinguished from leaf rust by its larger, elongated pustules primarily on stems and leaf sheaths, as opposed to smaller, rounder pustules on leaves.

name: Rice Blast
affected_hosts: Affects rice (Oryza sativa) and various wild grasses.
symptoms: Diamond-shaped lesions on leaves with gray centers and reddish-brown margins
Necrosis of nodes and neck leading to panicle breakage
Reduced grain filling and yield
conditions: High humidity, prolonged leaf wetness, and cool temperatures are ideal for disease development.
cycle: The fungus overwinters in infected plant debris or seeds, producing conidia that are dispersed by wind and rain, leading to new infections.
diagnosis: Identification of characteristic lesions and isolation of the pathogen from infected tissues confirms the disease.
impact: Considered one of the most destructive diseases of rice worldwide, capable of causing significant yield losses.
prevention: Utilizing resistant cultivars and proper nutrient management are key preventive measures.
organic: Balanced fertilization to avoid excessive nitrogen
ipm: Combines resistant varieties, cultural practices, and judicious fungicide application to manage disease outbreaks effectively.
geography: Present in all rice-growing regions globally, especially prevalent in Asia, Africa, and the Americas.
differential: Distinguished from other leaf spots by its characteristic diamond shape and the presence of a gray center with a dark border.

name: Maize Lethal Necrosis Disease (MLND)
scientific: Maize chlorotic mottle virus (MCMV) + a potyvirus (e.g., SCMV)
affected_hosts: Primarily affects maize, but other cereals can be susceptible.
symptoms: Severe stunting and chlorosis (yellowing) of leaves
Necrotic streaking on leaves and stem
Premature plant death and failure to produce cobs
conditions: High populations of insect vectors (thrips and aphids) and susceptible maize varieties favor rapid spread.
cycle: MCMV is primarily transmitted by thrips, while the potyvirus is transmitted by aphids; co-infection leads to the lethal necrosis syndrome.
diagnosis: Molecular tests (e.g., PCR, ELISA) are required to confirm the presence of both MCMV and the potyvirus.
impact: Causes severe yield losses, often 100% in affected fields, threatening food security in affected regions.
prevention: Using certified disease-free seeds and managing insect vectors are critical for prevention.
organic: Crop rotation and removal of alternative hosts
ipm: Focuses on resistant varieties, vector management, and strict phytosanitary measures to prevent disease introduction and spread.
geography: Predominantly found in East Africa, with potential for global spread to other maize-growing areas.
differential: Distinguished from single virus infections by the severe, synergistic symptoms including complete plant necrosis and premature death.

name: Tomato Late Blight
affected_hosts: Primarily affects tomato and potato plants, but can also infect other solanaceous crops.
symptoms: Water-soaked lesions on leaves and stems that rapidly turn brown/black
White, fuzzy fungal growth on the underside of leaves during humid conditions
Firm, dark brown lesions on fruits that become leathery
conditions: Cool, wet weather with high humidity and prolonged leaf wetness is highly conducive to rapid disease development.
cycle: The pathogen overwinters in infected tubers or plant debris, producing sporangia that are dispersed by wind and rain, leading to secondary infections.
diagnosis: Visual identification of characteristic lesions and white sporulation, confirmed by microscopic examination of sporangia.
impact: Can cause complete crop destruction within days under favorable conditions, leading to severe economic losses.
prevention: Planting resistant varieties, practicing good sanitation, and applying fungicides preventatively are essential.
organic: Proper plant spacing for air circulation
chemical: Fungicides containing chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or copper
Systemic fungicides for curative and protective action
ipm: Combines resistant cultivars, cultural practices, weather-based forecasting, and timely fungicide applications.
geography: Worldwide distribution, especially problematic in temperate and humid tropical regions.
differential: Distinguished from early blight by its rapid spread, larger water-soaked lesions, and white sporulation on leaf undersides.

name: Potato Common Scab
affected_hosts: Affects potatoes, radishes, carrots, and other root vegetables.
symptoms: Rough, corky lesions on the tuber surface, ranging from superficial to deep pitted
Raised or sunken brown spots on the skin
Reduced marketability due to cosmetic damage
conditions: Dry soil conditions during tuber initiation and high soil pH (above 5.2) favor disease development.
cycle: The bacteria survive in the soil and on infected plant debris, infecting young tubers through lenticels or wounds.
diagnosis: Visual inspection of characteristic scab lesions on tubers is usually sufficient for diagnosis.
impact: Primarily affects tuber quality and marketability, leading to significant economic losses for growers.
prevention: Using resistant varieties, maintaining acidic soil pH, and adequate soil moisture during tuberization are key.
organic: Green manure crops to lower soil pH
chemical: Soil fumigation in severe cases (limited use)
ipm: Involves choosing resistant varieties, crop rotation, soil pH management, and maintaining consistent soil moisture.
geography: Found in all potato-growing regions globally.
differential: Distinguished from powdery scab by the corky, rough texture of the lesions, lacking the powdery spore masses characteristic of powdery scab.

name: Citrus Greening (Huanglongbing - HLB)
affected_hosts: All citrus species and relatives, including orange, grapefruit, lemon, and tangerine.
symptoms: Asymmetrical yellowing of leaves (blotchy mottle) on one side of the midrib
Small, lopsided, bitter, and green-tipped fruits
Twig dieback and overall decline of tree vigor
conditions: Presence of the Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri) vector and infected trees are necessary for spread.
cycle: The bacteria are transmitted by the psyllid during feeding, colonizing the phloem of the tree and causing systemic decline.
diagnosis: Molecular tests (PCR) of leaf and stem tissue are required to confirm the presence of the bacterial pathogen.
impact: Considered the most destructive citrus disease worldwide, leading to tree decline, unmarketable fruit, and eventual death.
prevention: Strict psyllid control, removal of infected trees, and planting certified disease-free nursery stock are crucial.
ipm: Combines vector management, removal of infected trees, use of disease-free plant material, and quarantine measures.
geography: Widespread in Asia, Africa, North and South America, particularly devastating in Florida and Brazil.
differential: Distinguished from nutrient deficiencies by the asymmetrical, blotchy yellowing on leaves, which does not follow a symmetrical pattern.

name: Banana Fusarium Wilt (Panama Disease) TR4
scientific: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense Tropical Race 4
affected_hosts: Highly virulent on Cavendish banana cultivars, but can affect other banana and plantain varieties.
symptoms: Yellowing and wilting of older leaves from the margins, progressing to younger leaves
Splitting of pseudostems and eventual collapse of the plant
Reddish-brown discoloration in the vascular tissue of the rhizome
conditions: Warm soil temperatures and contaminated soil are highly conducive to disease development and spread.
cycle: The fungus survives in soil for decades, infecting plants through roots and colonizing the vascular system, leading to wilting.
diagnosis: Visual symptoms, confirmed by characteristic vascular discoloration in the pseudostem and rhizome, and laboratory isolation of the fungus.
impact: Lethal to susceptible banana varieties, with no effective chemical control, threatening global banana production.
prevention: Strict quarantine, use of disease-free planting material, and resistant varieties are the only effective measures.
organic: Use of resistant or tolerant varieties
chemical: Soil fumigation is not practical or effective for large areas
ipm: Relies heavily on exclusion, sanitation, resistant varieties, and containment strategies to prevent spread.
geography: Originated in Southeast Asia, now spread to Africa, the Middle East, and parts of Latin America.
differential: Distinguished from bacterial wilt by the absence of bacterial ooze and the specific reddish-brown vascular discoloration.

name: Coffee Leaf Rust
affected_hosts: Primarily affects coffee species, especially Arabica coffee (Coffea arabica).
symptoms: Small, yellow-orange powdery spots on the underside of leaves
Spots enlarge and turn bright orange, eventually becoming necrotic
Premature leaf drop, defoliation, and reduced berry production
conditions: Warm temperatures, high humidity, and prolonged leaf wetness promote spore germination and infection.
cycle: Spores are dispersed by wind and rain from infected leaves, germinating and penetrating the leaf through stomata.
diagnosis: Visual identification of characteristic yellow-orange powdery pustules on the underside of leaves.
impact: Can cause severe defoliation, leading to reduced yields and tree debilitation, resulting in significant economic losses.
prevention: Planting resistant varieties and timely application of fungicides are crucial for management.
organic: Proper shade management to reduce leaf wetness
chemical: Systemic fungicides (triazoles) for protection and eradication
ipm: Integrates resistant varieties, cultural practices (shade, nutrition), and strategic fungicide applications based on monitoring.
geography: Present in nearly all coffee-growing regions worldwide, especially problematic in Central and South America.
differential: Distinguished from other leaf spots by the characteristic powdery, orange pustules on the underside of leaves.
